title: Technical deep dive: model tuning (Llama/Mistral/Qwen) + ROPE/MoE
summary: Redwood SEs walked HelixAI through runtime performance tuning for Llama/Mistral/Qwen families with focus on ROPE scaling, MoE routing costs, KV-cache sizing, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Discussed benchmarks, fallbacks, and next steps: run customer-specific bench with 2k token workflow, share detailed perf matrix, provide on-prem deployment checklist and KMS notes.

KV cache sizing and eviction policies
Quantization impact (int8/4-bit) on throughput and quality
VPC / on-prem integration and networking considerations

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-04 14:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lucia Gomez (Redwood SE), Maria Vasquez (HelixAI), Tom Harding (CTO), Raj Singh (SRE), Priya Malhotra (ML Research)

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're hoping to cover model-specific tuning — llama, mistral, qwen, also rope scale and moe routing costs. can everyone hear ok?
00:06 Maria Vasquez: yes thanks alex, loud and clear. our goal is to understand runtime tradeoffs and what to expect on our dedicated cluster if we push 2k token generations at 200 qps bursts.
00:15 Samir Patel: got it. i'll start with a high-level then drill into kv-cache, batching, and where rope scaling bites you. lucia will show a couple of micro-benchmarks.
00:28 Lucia Gomez: quick note, some model names in my slides get transcribed weird so i'll say qwen 2x as "q-win" sometimes, sorry in advance.
00:35 Tom Harding: ha, no worries. we've also seen routing costs spike on some MoE runs — curious how you model that.
00:42 Samir Patel: yeah that's a core part. MoE routing is cheap on the forward pass but the memory and kernel dispatch overhead can kill throughput if you don't batch routing decisions. for small batch sizes routing overhead becomes nontrivial.
00:55 Raj Singh: are we assuming GPU persistent kernels or multi-process worker pools? we tend to run multi-process right now for isolation.
01:03 Samir Patel: good q. Redwood Dedicated supports both; persistent kernels with a single process per GPU get you best latency and throughput. multi-process gives isolation but you pay context switch and memcpy overheads. we can quantify for your infra.
01:18 Lucia Gomez: (slide) here's a comparison: Llama-like dense transformer, Mistral with eval-optimized blocks, and Qwen which has slightly different attention layout and more aggressive rope variants in newer checkpoints.
01:30 Samir Patel: ROPE scaling — short summary: as you increase sequence length beyond training recipy, you can see phase misalignment and slow degradation. models with relative positional encodings (rope) may need scaling tricks; we often apply rope scaling factors or use rotary reinit to reduce drift.
01:45 Priya Malhotra: we've observed hallucination increase after 1k tokens in Llama-derivatives; is that rope drift or KV cache evictions?
01:53 Samir Patel: could be both. rope drift affects attention weighting; kv-cache size and eviction policy affects whether old context is retained. if you evict too aggressively to save memory you'll lose context.
02:05 Maria Vasquez: what's a practical recipe? we want to keep 2k context with good latency under 200 qps bursts.
02:12 Lucia Gomez: recipe: use int8 quantization for dense parts, configure per-model kv-cache per GPU to hold full 2k for active sessions, and use continuous batching with max batch window 20-40ms. that keeps P99 latency within your SLOs in most cases.
02:30 Tom Harding: int8 — is quality hit acceptable for instruction style outputs? we've benchmarked against our eval set and saw ~0.8% decline for some tasks.
02:38 Samir Patel: depends on the model; qwen generally tolerates int8 better than some llama forks. we recommend running a small eval suite. for critical tasks we recommend mixed quantization: int8 on feedforward + fp16 attention, or Q4 for layers that are quality-sensitive.
02:55 Raj Singh: about KV cache sizing — we have 8 A100s per pod. what's realistic per-GPU cache RAM to hold 2k context for a 13B model?
03:04 Lucia Gomez: ballpark: 13B dense ~ 4-6 GB per GPU for kv when storing full past keys/values at 2k. MoE increases that because of expert routing but experts are sharded; still expect +20-40% memory for routing metadata and per-expert caches.
03:20 Samir Patel: note on MoE: routing overhead can be amortized if you batch routing decisions. but if you have high-cardinality small sessions (lots of small interactive calls) you pay routing per-request. that's where we see throughput drop.
03:36 Maria Vasquez: ok so for our interactive assistant sessions (median 300 tokens, tail 2k), we need dynamic policies. do you have autoscale or fallback models?
03:44 Alex Chen: yes, smart routing — policy-based fallback to a smaller dense variant in spikes, or degrade to cached responses for repeat prefixes. we can auto-fallback from MoE to a dense 13B model with lower token cost.
03:58 Tom Harding: what's the observed latency delta when falling back from MoE to dense?
04:05 Samir Patel: depends on model sizes; routing and expert dispatch adds 5-25ms in optimized path, but with bad batching it can add 50-200ms. dense path generally more predictable.
04:20 Raj Singh: networking implications for VPC/on-prem: we have a 10 Gbps interconnect and strict egress filters. anything special needed?
04:27 Lucia Gomez: on-prem we recommend pinning traffic inside the VPC, use private control plane, and ensure NVLink or RDMA for multi-GPU shards. also KMS in a private subnet for key ops. we sent a checklist earlier but will re-share.
04:44 Maria Vasquez: yes please resend. also curious about cold starts for large models with kv cache warmup.
04:51 Samir Patel: cold starts depend on whether you keep model resident. for Dedicated we keep warm processes; cold start primarily when model isn't resident or after eviction. warmup strategies: prefetch embeddings and initial KV pages, or keep a tiny warm pool.
05:05 Lucia Gomez: demo snippet — here's a micro-benchmark we ran: Qwen 14B int8 dense vs Qwen 14B fp16 at varying batch sizes and seq=512/2048. 
05:16 Lucia Gomez: results: at seq=512, int8 gets ~1.8x throughput; at 2048 int8 wins ~2-2.2x but shows slightly higher variance at P99. Llama 13B int8 gains are smaller ~1.4x at long sequences.
05:33 Priya Malhotra: variance at P99 — could that be due to NVMe-backed kv spilling?
05:40 Samir Patel: yes if you spill kv to device memory or host; that's a big performance cliff. avoid spilling with right cache sizing or use local NVMe with async prefetch.
05:50 Maria Vasquez: for our Dedicated plan, are we able to tune eviction thresholds per customer?
05:56 Alex Chen: yes per-route settings in Console, and policy-based retention. we can set cold eviction policy per-model and per-customer.
06:06 Tom Harding: instrumentation — we need token-level cost and per-model P99 traces. is that exposed?
06:12 Lucia Gomez: Console exposes token cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, and tracing hooks. we can add custom spans if you want to correlate with your SRE logs.
06:22 Raj Singh: on security, KMS integration and HSM — is the key material ever at rest in Redwood?
06:28 Alex Chen: for Private deployments, keys are customer-managed; Redwood control plane doesn't hold raw key material. we can support your KMS or HSM via KMIP or cloud KMS connectors.
06:39 Maria Vasquez: fine. can you also share SOC 2 / ISO artifacts?
06:43 Alex Chen: yes we'll include security pack in next email.
06:47 Lucia Gomez: back to MoE routing costs — we model cost as base_token_cost + routing_overhead * active_experts + extra_memory_tax. typically routing_overhead ~ 5-30% depending on batch and sparsity.
06:59 Tom Harding: can you show an example cost calc?
07:02 Samir Patel: quick example: dense 13B base cost x. MoE 13B with 16 experts, effective FLOPs can be 1.3-1.8x due to routing and dispatch; with poor batching that moves to 2x. we price Dedicated reserveds with an explicit routing uplift.
07:20 Maria Vasquez: good to have the model. also rope scaling — do you offer automatic rope rescaling at runtime?
07:27 Lucia Gomez: currently we offer recommended transforms during model onboarding: rope_scale factors and position re-mapping. automated runtime rescaling is experimental because it can change model semantics. we prefer staged rollout and evals.
07:41 Priya Malhotra: any hacks for reducing rope drift?
07:44 Samir Patel: options: linear rope scaling, interpolation strategies, or periodic position counter reset combined with cache segmentation. each has tradeoffs. we usually test on your eval suite to pick the least degradation.
07:57 Raj Singh: about batching windows: you mentioned 20-40ms, what if our product requires sub-50ms P50?
08:05 Lucia Gomez: then you lower batch window to 8-12ms with more aggressive per-request routing limits, accept lower throughput, or use more reserved capacity. also continuous batching with partial flush is helpful.
08:17 Tom Harding: are those knobs exposed in API or Console?
08:20 Alex Chen: both: API params for latency-sensitive routes and Console presets. we can set a per-route latency SLO and autoscale rules.
08:31 Maria Vasquez: let's talk concrete next steps please.
08:34 Alex Chen: summarize: we will run a bespoke bench on your sample prompts for 512 and 2k tokens, include MoE-enabled and dense variants, compare int8/q4/fp16, and produce a perf+cost matrix. we'll also send the on-prem checklist and KMS notes.
08:48 Maria Vasquez: ok sounds good. one more question: for flows with heavy retrieval and long context expansions, is it better to chunk and use compressed embeddings or keep full rope context?
08:58 Samir Patel: retrieval-compressed embeddings plus a summary in KV-cache is often better. long raw context with rope scaling risks drift and increases kv memory. we can show a hybrid pattern.
09:14 Tom Harding: thanks all. any final clarifications?
09:18 Alex Chen: not from us. lucia, samir — you'll own the bench and docs.
09:23 Lucia Gomez: yep. we'll follow up with times for the bench run.
09:27 Maria Vasquez: thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes about transcript quality: some words transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "qwen" as "q-win", "ROPE" occasionally as "ropee"), speaker overlap labeled occasionally as single speaker.

Shared artifacts referenced: perf-matrix.xlsx (link shared in chat), onprem_deploy_checklist.pdf (will be sent), KMS-integration-notes.md (will be attached).
